BBC, 25 Nov 2026 06:09 GMT

'Hope' as Black Friday ad ban launches in UK first

The tradition falls on the fourth Thursday of every November

Low body shot of person holding four shopping bags on a busy street

The first city in the UK to ban advertisements for Black Friday and fast fashion sales has sparked \"hope\" among independent retailers.

The Green-run Bristol City Council voted in September to ban the promotions on council-owned billboards as part of the authority's efforts to fight climate change.

Ahead of Black Friday, some independent businesses said the move could help their trade, while a Gloucestershire parent warned the annual mass sale is often overplayed.

Rushka Gray, who works at Bristol Gloucester Road's independent UStudio, said: \"I think it's a really good start...it just gives independents maybe a little bit more of a head start. I hope that it makes a difference.\"

Jamie Birch, also known as SavvyJamie, a content creator from Gloucestershire who shares money-saving tips online, said she is \"really careful\" on Black Friday as it is \"[easy to] get sucked into thinking something is a good deal and it's not\".

\"I think that's something that some people forget, a deal is only a deal if you were going to buy it anyway,\" she added.

Rather than buying brand new Christmas gifts on Black Friday, the mother-of-three prefers to buy second-hand and support small, independent businesses - which she hopes will benefit from the ban by evening the playing field.

She said: \"I think when you shop small you're literally putting food on someone's table [and] paying for someone's child's swimming lessons rather than putting money in massive corporate machines.\"

Content creator and mother SavvyJamie said it can be easy to fall for Black Friday deals

Steve English, owner of an independent shop called Cooshti, said his business was one of the first to start Black Friday sales in Bristol.

The annual event originated in the United States in the 1980s before spreading to UK stores in 2010.

Described as a \"frenzy\" by English, he also acknowledged that it enables \"the consumer gets money off before Christmas and the businesses get much-needed turnover in that quarter\".

English said: \"Mostly I would advertise Black Friday digitally, and if I wanted to put a sign in my window, it's not council-owned property so I would be able to.

\"The brand and the stock that we sell, the whole idea is really against fast fashion.

\"We sell stuff with longevity and quality garments that are not in that fast fashion bracket,\" he added.

Cooshti was one of Bristol's first stores to launch Black Friday sales

Sarah Burns, head of sustainability and customer engagement at Bristol Waste Company, said that moving away from buying items we do not need is the best solution to protect the planet.

Research from Zable, a consumer finance platform, found that 35% of UK adults regret impulse buys on Black Friday, purchases which Burns said \"end up in the bin\".

\"This ban isn't about attacking shoppers. It's a real opportunity for us to rethink how we shop, especially in the lead-up to Christmas.

\"When something is too cheap and too easy to throw away, we all pay the price – environmentally, financially, and sadly sometimes physically,\" she added.

British people, particularly teens and young adults, are having less or no sex compared to past generations, but lots are watching porn and sexting, a major study suggests.

It is the first time The National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles' (Natsal) research into general public sex lives has asked about online behaviours.

The latest results were published in The Lancet and were based on a survey of 6,700 people aged 16–59 who were selected at random across Britain.

Energy bills will rise by 26% for millions of households in January, the highest rate in nearly four years, after a surge in gas prices sparked by the Iran war.

Isaac, a student at Durham University, said he had no choice but to keep the heating in his student house on 'constantly' due to poor insulation, and he was not looking forward to the price increase.

In the Autumn budget, the government announced a one-off payment of £100 for households in council bands A to D, 'half a weekly shop' according to Isaac.
